request.system:
You are assisting with the qualitative analysis of interview data from a study of frontline hotel employees' work experiences. You will receive one passage from an interview transcript. Code the passage as a qualitative researcher would in first-order coding, and complete the coding form below.

About the passage
- The passage begins with brief details about the interviewee: role, gender and years in the job.
- Lines marked "Interviewer:" are the interviewer's questions. Lines marked "Interviewee:" are the interviewee's answers.
- Some passages contain two excerpts from the same interview, marked [Earlier in the interview] and [Later in the interview].

The coding form
1. codes: Give between 3 and 6 first-order codes. Each code has a short label of 2 to 6 words, kept close to the interviewee's own language, and one supporting quote. Each quote must be copied word for word from the passage, without any change, and must be no longer than 30 words.
2. interpretation: In one or two sentences, in your own words, state what the interviewee is communicating in this passage.
3. tone: The overall tone of the interviewee's account. Choose one: positive, negative, mixed or neutral.
4. confidence: An integer from 0 to 100 indicating how confident you are that your interpretation is accurate.

Respond only with a JSON object that follows the schema provided. Write in English.
request.user:
Interviewee details: Front-desk receptionist, female, 3rd year

Interviewer: The hotel switched to a new front-desk system this year. How have you found it?

Interviewee: The new system was rolled out across the whole group. At the training, the instructor said it would raise efficiency by thirty percent, and the interface really does look better than the old one: the colours and icons are all very clear. Our supervisor also said at a meeting that we should embrace change and stop comparing everything with the old system, and everyone nodded. But these days, the first thing I do when I start my shift is copy out all of the day’s reservations by hand, in a hardcover notebook I bought myself: room number, name, arrival time, deposit, nothing left out. At handover I also go through the notebook with the colleague on the next shift to make sure nothing’s been missed. Before I leave, I photograph the in-house guest list in the system page by page and keep the photos on my phone, in a folder I set up specially. I’ve got over two hundred of them by now. Once last month the system froze, and there were a dozen or so people queuing in the lobby. One guest had a flight to catch and kept looking at his watch. So I went by my notebook and assigned rooms first, wrote out the deposit slips by hand, and once the system came back I entered everything again, one by one. I was at it until nearly midnight. That guest with the flight ended up leaving with a deposit slip I’d written by hand. After that day, our supervisor went to a stationery shop and bought the same kind of notebook, and she keeps it in her drawer. She didn’t tell anyone. Our night-shift colleagues still have the old system’s technician on WeChat, and when something goes wrong they go to him first rather than calling the new system’s support hotline. A few days ago the manager asked everyone how it was going, and we all said it was going fine. The new system’s interface really does look nice. Everyone agrees on that.
